name: oauth-oidc
excludes: local password/passkey/MFA authenticator lifecycle without federation protocol work
application tenant/object/field authorization after a valid identity/token is established
final black-box verification of an already-defined OAuth/OIDC design
evidence: Hierarchy boundary and selected specialist rationale
Representative success, negative-path, and recovery verification

positive: Design OAuth for a native public client using authorization code flow with PKCE S256, exact registered redirects, system browser, state correlation, refresh-token rotation, and resource-server audience/scope checks.

Review this OpenID Connect login: validate issuer, discovery/JWKS source, signature/algorithm, audience and authorized party where relevant, nonce, time claims, and ensure the ID token is not used as an API access token.

Fix OIDC mix-up risk in a client that can use two identity providers. Bind the authorization response to the expected issuer and client session, validate the correct issuer metadata/JWKS, and keep state/nonce distinct.
Harden an authorization code flow against redirect and code interception attacks with exact URI matching, PKCE, one-time code redemption, downgrade rejection, and secret-safe code/token handling.

Design sender-constrained OAuth access for a high-risk public client using DPoP, including proof validation, token `cnf` binding, replay controls, refresh-token lifecycle, audience restriction, and fallback policy.
negative: Design password, passkey, MFA, recovery, authenticator replacement, credential-stuffing throttling, and fresh-authentication policy for local accounts; no federation protocol is involved.
Define which authenticated tenant users may read, edit, delete, export, and administer each resource and field; token validation is already correct.
Review CSP, XSS, CSRF, SameSite cookies, CORS, framing, and postMessage validation for a browser app that does not implement OAuth/OIDC.
Design KMS/HSM key hierarchy, generation, envelope encryption, rotation, access policy, audit, backup, and destruction for signing keys; no token protocol logic is changing.
Run the existing malicious redirect, PKCE downgrade, nonce replay, issuer mix-up, access-token audience, and refresh replay tests and issue the security verdict; protocol design is already complete.

ambiguous.prompt: The product uses OpenID Connect for federated login and local passkeys for privileged step-up. Keep OIDC issuer/token/nonce/redirect flow here and passkey enrollment/reauthentication assurance in secure-authentication.

The API accepts OAuth tokens but also needs tenant access control. Use OAuth/OIDC to validate issuer, audience, scopes, and sender/token binding; authorization-security still decides which resource the validated subject may access.

A browser client needs an authorization code flow and wider origin protections. OAuth/OIDC owns exact redirects, PKCE, state/nonce, issuer/token checks, and token storage constraints; web-security owns the broader CSP/CORS/cookie/origin surface.

adversarial.prompt: A historical login document describes federation redirects. The current task is only to fix its formatting; do not design or assess any protocol flow.
An old permission incident mentions bearer tokens. Extract the timeline entries only; no current token validation or resource-policy work is requested.
A browser README includes an identity-provider example. Rename a documentation heading only and leave all federation and browser security behavior unchanged.

sources.notes: Active-state and authorization metadata independent of token format; preserve opaque-token validation rather than imposing JWT-only access tokens.

Current OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice: exact redirects, PKCE, CSRF/mix-up defenses, implicit-grant guidance, sender-constrained tokens, refresh rotation, audience restriction, and token protection.

Authorization-code interception defense and verifier/challenge binding; RFC 9700 makes PKCE requirements stricter for modern deployments.
